title: Time Repair: The Missing Reformation
subtitle: Find the gap · Trace the cause · Repair Gutenberg · See the record

inventionRescue.fiction: Four-week alternate-history investigation: the time archive contains Luther’s 1517 Ninety-five Theses, but the printed debate that helped the controversy travel is missing. Students first infer what did not happen, then use alternate newspapers and interviews to trace the fictional cause to a failed European printing system. Week 3 moves back to Gutenberg’s Mainz workshop to repair and learn the press. Week 4 returns to documented 1517–1518 evidence. The broken timeline is a teaching counterfactual, not a claim that one machine alone caused the Protestant Reformation.
inventionRescue.modelNote: Timeline cards, newspaper issues, and interviews are constructed classroom evidence, not recordings or newly discovered documents. The three press repairs are qualitative models, not measured historical speeds, routes, or recipes. Gutenberg’s mid-1450s workshop is an earlier prerequisite in this story; he did not print Luther’s theses or meet Luther. The real-history comparison separates documented editions from invented witnesses and keeps religious change, institutions, rulers, language, and people’s choices visible.

sources.title: The problem of printing
sources.detail: Manuscript ink did not adhere adequately to metal type. Printing required suitable ink and consistent pressure. Gutenberg’s precise equipment is not completely known.

sources.title: A book made by many hands
sources.detail: Gutenberg and collaborators produced their Bible in Mainz in the mid-1450s. Printed copies still involved hand finishing. A working press depended on skilled people, supplies, and financial support.

sources.title: Printing before Gutenberg
sources.detail: Jikji was printed with movable metal type in Korea in 1377. This mission concerns a European workshop, not the first printing anywhere in the world.

sources.title: Luther’s Ninety-five Theses · 1517 printed edition
sources.detail: The Library of Congress describes Luther’s Latin propositions for debate about indulgences and the part printing played in their wider circulation. This surviving Nuremberg edition is evidence of a real printed document; our workshop models are reconstructions.

sources.title: A surviving Basel printing of the theses
sources.detail: The Gruber Rare Books Collection identifies Adam Petri’s Basel edition of 1517 and explains the dispute over indulgences. Luther was a Catholic monk and theology professor seeking debate; the later Reformation was not already a completed plan in the document.

sources.title: Printing and the circulation of ideas
sources.detail: IEEE’s historical inquiry unit identifies editions printed in Leipzig, Nuremberg, and Basel in late 1517. The three model workshops represent printing centers, not a documented route taken by a single messenger.

sources.title: Martin Luther as Priest, Heretic and Outlaw
sources.detail: The Library of Congress guide places Luther’s 1517 debate in the context of the earlier movable-type press and explains how German presses helped his writing travel.

weeks.title: Find what did not happen
weeks.goal: Infer the missing printed debate from a broken timeline and surviving clues before naming a cause.
evidence: Inspected timeline records with one unexplained gap
A selected candidate tested against every clue

weeks.title: Find what caused the gap
weeks.goal: Use alternate newspapers and interviews to isolate the failed printing process without treating one witness as the whole explanation.
evidence: Two columns inspected in every alternate issue
Witness accounts paired with physical objects
A press-trail explanation that separates evidence from inference

weeks.title: Repair and learn Gutenberg
weeks.goal: Study how movable type, ink, pressure, and skilled crafts combine, then repair the failed press in controlled trials.

A diagnosis that identifies the tested fault and its limits

sessions.title: Find the missing event
sessions.task: The archive jumps from Luther’s manuscript to a quiet winter. Inspect each record, place a candidate in the gap, and test it against the clues. You are not told what disappeared; the timeline has to convince you.
sessions.goal: Infer that a printed debate is the missing event while separating the historical Ninety-five Theses from our fictional absence of circulation.
sessions.product: A tested candidate for the missing event and a clue-by-clue timeline record.
sessions.historicalNote: Martin Luther wrote the Ninety-five Theses in 1517 as propositions for debate about indulgences. The Library of Congress record identifies surviving 1517 printings and describes how printing helped the text spread. This first scene asks students to infer that missing spread from a fictional broken archive; it does not claim the posting story or later Reformation had one automatic cause.
sessions.question: Which event best explains the hole? What evidence shows the idea existed, and what evidence shows its wider printed circulation is the part missing?

timeline.title: The hole in the record

nodes.label: Luther writes
nodes.detail: A Latin set of propositions is prepared for an academic debate about indulgences.
nodes.signal: The idea exists before any press run.

nodes.label: Manuscripts travel
nodes.detail: Handwritten pages can leave Wittenberg one at a time.
nodes.signal: Travel survives in the broken record.

nodes.label: The copy gap
nodes.detail: The archive shows no usable printed editions reaching other workshops.
nodes.signal: This blank needs a candidate, not a guess from a title.

nodes.label: Debate stays local
nodes.detail: Readers outside Wittenberg report no shared printed text to compare.
nodes.signal: A consequence should follow the missing link.

candidates.label: Printed Theses circulate
candidates.detail: Repeatable copies carry the debate beyond Wittenberg.

candidates.label: A royal order arrives
candidates.detail: A ruler announces a decision without a copied debate.

candidates.label: A trade road opens
candidates.detail: Travel improves, but no new page is multiplied.

sessions.title: Hear the quiet debate
sessions.task: Interview a bookseller, a university student, and a church visitor from the alternate timeline. Hear each account, inspect the object they carried, and weigh what their three viewpoints can—and cannot—prove.
sessions.goal: Use independent witnesses and physical evidence to confirm the missing circulation without turning a fictional interview into a primary source.
sessions.product: A witness board linking three alternate accounts to the missing printed debate.
sessions.historicalNote: These witnesses are fictional teaching voices. They represent different positions a student can compare: a seller sees supply, a student sees debate, and a church visitor sees local notice. The documented history is supplied separately through the source cards and the final-week comparison.
sessions.question: What do all three voices share? Which detail is an observation, and which is your inference about why the debate did not spread?

interview.title: Voices from a quiet debate

witnesses.name: Anna
witnesses.statement: I can carry a manuscript, but no shop sends me a stack of the same page. Customers ask for a copy I cannot show them.
witnesses.clue: Supply is thin even when a handwritten page can arrive.

witnesses.name: Matthias
witnesses.statement: We argue about the propositions from memory. No identical printed page reaches our table, so the wording keeps changing.
witnesses.clue: Without repeatable copies, a public argument is hard to compare.

witnesses.name: Greta
witnesses.statement: I hear a local notice, then the trail goes quiet. A messenger can carry one page, but not a roomful of readers.
witnesses.clue: Local speech remains while the wider printed network is absent.

interview.answer: Independent voices point to a missing multiplication step: the manuscript exists, but a reliable press does not make enough matching copies.

sessions.title: Read the alternate newspapers
sessions.task: Open three newspaper issues from the world without a working press. Inspect two columns in every issue, compare the editions, and trace the physical failure they keep circling without naming.
sessions.goal: Identify the failed multiplication process as the cause of the missing printed debate, while distinguishing a newspaper’s report from tested material evidence.
sessions.product: A press-trail reading supported by inspected alternate newspaper columns.
sessions.historicalNote: These issues are fictional composites. Newspapers did not exist in this exact form in Luther’s 1517 controversy; they are a visual investigation device that lets students compare supply, rumor, and material clues before repairing the press.
sessions.question: Which repeated clue points to a process failure rather than a lack of interest? What still happens in this alternate world?

newspaper.title: News from a world without copies

editions.headline: One manuscript, many requests
editions.subhead: A bookseller waits for a repeatable page
columns: Metal type leaves a faint mark.
editions.signal: The issue reports demand but no reliable supply.

editions.headline: Debate changes with each copy
editions.subhead: Students compare memories instead of pages
columns: A press pull fails on metal.
editions.signal: The issue separates an idea from its reproducible form.

editions.headline: News travels, then stops
columns: A second room hears a rumor.
editions.signal: The issue links the social symptom to a physical clue.

newspaper.answer: The alternate reports converge on a broken multiplication step: handwriting and speech survive, but ink will not make reliable copies from metal type.

sessions.title: Interview the failed workshop
sessions.task: Question three workshop voices about the old failure. Hear each account, inspect the object left on the bench, and weigh the evidence before deciding which physical cause is worth testing in Week 3.
sessions.goal: Trace the alternate timeline’s cause to ink adhesion and linked press crafts, without treating fictional witnesses as proof of what Gutenberg’s exact workshop looked like.
sessions.product: A cause diagnosis that names a testable fault and its limits.
sessions.historicalNote: The date points to Gutenberg’s mid-fifteenth-century Mainz context. The people and objects in this interview are teaching reconstructions. The next week tests the material claim instead of accepting a witness’s story.
sessions.question: Which physical clue can be tested? What would an interview alone fail to establish about Gutenberg’s real workshop?

interview.title: Voices from the failed shop

witnesses.name: Marta
witnesses.statement: The old ink looks dark on paper, but it beads on the metal letters. We kept changing the recipe without keeping a clean comparison.
witnesses.clue: Adhesion to paper is not the same as adhesion to metal.

witnesses.name: Peter
witnesses.statement: The letters can be arranged, but loose pieces shift if the frame does not hold them together.
witnesses.clue: A repeatable page needs a frame as well as type.

witnesses.name: Jonas
witnesses.statement: I can carry a page to another town. I cannot carry enough pages to make a public debate by hand.
witnesses.clue: Travel is not the same as multiplication.

interview.answer: The testable cause is a linked material failure: ink beads on metal type, while a reliable frame and pressure are also needed for repeatable copies.

sessions.title: Test the failed press
sessions.task: The interviews named a material clue. Test the numbered inks on paper and metal, change pressure one variable at a time, and pull clean proofs. The press opens here because this is the repair week.
sessions.goal: Diagnose the physical failure with controlled material and pressure comparisons.
sessions.product: Paired material tests and proofs showing which repair conditions work.
sessions.historicalNote: This is a qualitative reconstruction of a mid-fifteenth-century European press, not Gutenberg’s exact machine. The tested repair supplies a model for how later printers could multiply texts; it does not prove a single-cause explanation for the Reformation.
sessions.question: Which change fixed the physical symptom? Which historical consequences remain an inference?

sessions.title: Build the Gutenberg system
sessions.task: Fit the frame, mold, ink ball, and screw into the press. Operate each craft contribution, compare a failed assembly with a clean one, and explain why the repair is a system rather than one magic part.
sessions.goal: Learn how linked crafts make movable-type printing repeatable and repair the assembled system.
sessions.product: An assembled press and trial evidence showing what each craft contributes.
sessions.historicalNote: Gutenberg and collaborators produced a Bible in Mainz in the mid-1450s. The scene is a teaching reconstruction; the exact tools, counts, and sequence are simplified. Earlier printing traditions in East Asia remain part of the wider history.
sessions.question: Which parts had to cooperate before a future printer could multiply Luther’s text? What does the model leave uncertain?

sessions.title: Read the history that happened
sessions.task: Open the surviving-edition desk. Inspect two columns in each historical issue, compare Leipzig, Nuremberg, and Basel, and trace what the real printed record can show about the spread of Luther’s debate.
sessions.goal: Use surviving print evidence to compare the repaired model with the documented circulation of the Ninety-five Theses.
sessions.product: A source-grounded reading of what printing changed and what it could not decide alone.
sessions.historicalNote: The Library of Congress record describes a Nuremberg printing of the Ninety-five Theses and notes editions in Leipzig, Nuremberg, and Basel by the end of 1517. These cards summarize source evidence; they are not newly discovered newspaper issues.
sessions.question: What do the surviving editions establish? Which parts of the later Protestant Reformation still require people, institutions, conflict, and choice?

newspaper.title: The record in surviving editions

editions.headline: Ninety-five Theses printed
editions.subhead: A surviving edition preserves the Latin propositions
columns: The text was prepared for debate.
The page could travel beyond Wittenberg.
A printed copy is evidence, not conversion.
editions.signal: A surviving Nuremberg edition documents a real printed text.

editions.headline: The debate reaches another press
editions.subhead: An unnamed printer joins the circulation
editions.signal: The record lists Leipzig among the early German printings.

editions.headline: A third workshop carries the text
editions.subhead: The printed controversy crosses a region
editions.signal: Basel is another documented early printing center.

newspaper.answer: Surviving 1517 editions show that printing widened the debate; the Reformation’s later direction also depended on institutions, rulers, religious arguments, language, and people’s choices.

sessions.title: Compare the repaired timeline
sessions.task: Return to the timeline. Inspect the documented events, switch between the repaired model and the historical record, place the best explanation in the final gap, and test whether your story leaves room for other causes.
sessions.goal: Explain the relationship between the repaired invention and the real historical spread of Luther’s Ninety-five Theses without making printing the only cause.
sessions.product: A final timeline comparison distinguishing documented evidence, model results, and counterfactual inference.
sessions.historicalNote: The historical record supports early print circulation of Luther’s propositions and the role of printing in the Reformation’s rapid spread. The repaired timeline is still a counterfactual model. It helps students reason about a condition of possibility; it cannot replay a world that never existed.
sessions.question: Which parts of your repaired story are documented, which came from the model, and which remain a reasonable but unproven counterfactual?

nodes.label: Controversy expands

nodes.detail: Our broken timeline removes reliable multiplication and shows a quieter, more local debate.
nodes.signal: This is an inference experiment, not a historical document.
